I have been a stage manager for eleven years, and for most of that time I was the person who stands behind the curtain with a headset and a stopwatch. Nobody in the audience knows my name, and that is exactly how it should be. But here is something that took me years to understand. Every show has a go-to person who is not on the call sheet as anything special. On our show it was a sound assistant called Marcos. He was the one who knew which microphone had a weak cable, which singer needed water before every take, and which door to the stage got stuck in the rain. One Thursday he was sick, and somebody else had to step in. The show still happened. But in about ten minutes, all of us discovered how much of the evening had been sitting quietly on one person. The next week, we wrote down everything that Marcos knew. It took four pages.

When I started as a music director, I thought the hard part would be the music. It was not. The hard part was the handoffs: the arrangement which leaves my desk on Monday and arrives at the band on Wednesday, the click track that goes to the video team, the lyric sheet that goes to the captions. Every one of those is a place where something can get lost. So we made one rule, and it changed everything. Every file has a point of contact, one person who answers questions about it, and that person keeps the others in the loop. It sounds like paperwork, and it is the opposite. Before the rule, people guessed. After the rule, people asked. And I learned to delegate properly for the first time, because I finally knew who was doing what, not only what needed to be done.

Pedro says that the host is the person who everybody remembers. He explains that the people who make the show possible work behind the scenes. He says that their go-to person is a sound assistant who knows every cable. He adds that the weakest point is the handoff, the moment when work passes to the next team. He says that every file now has a point of contact who keeps everybody in the loop. Then he thanks the people whose work usually goes unnoticed.
